scenarios.title: Cyber Security: Teach the World
scenarios.context: You have been chosen to deliver a 10-minute cyber security presentation to an audience of your choice — it could be other students, parents, or younger children. Over the next 6 weeks you will become an expert in cyber security threats, learn how to stay safe online, and build a professional presentation that could genuinely protect the people who watch it. By the end, you will know more about cyber security than most adults.
scenarios.subjectPrompt: Who will you present to? (e.g. Year 7 students, Year 6 students, parents, a mixed audience)

1.starterQuestion:
Look at these passwords:

   fluffy123
   P@ssw0rd!
   correct-horse-battery-staple
   Xk#9mQ2$vL

Which do you think is the STRONGEST? Which is the WEAKEST? Be ready to explain your answer.

keyTerms.def: A secret string of characters used to verify your identity
The process of proving you are who you claim to be
A second check on top of your password — e.g. a code sent to your phone
When a hacker tries millions of password combinations automatically
When a hacker tries common words and phrases as passwords

1.exampleTitle: How long to crack a password?
1.exampleBody: Password cracking software can try billions of combinations per second. Here is how long common passwords take to crack:
1.exampleCode:
"password"         → Instantly cracked
"Password1"        → Less than 1 second
"P@ssword1"        → About 3 minutes
"Tr0ub4dor&3"      → About 3 days
"correct-horse-staple" → 550 years
"Xk#9mQ2$vL"       → 34 million years

Key lesson: LENGTH beats complexity every time.
1.defaultNote: Today we're focusing on passwords — the first line of defence. Make sure students attempt the strength checker task practically.

2.starterQuestion:
You receive this email:

'Dear Customer, Your account has been suspended. Click here immediately to verify your details or your account will be deleted within 24 hours. — Security Team'

What are THREE things that might tell you this is fake?

keyTerms.def: A fake email or message designed to trick you into giving away personal information
A targeted phishing attack aimed at a specific person using personal details
Manipulating people psychologically to get them to reveal information or take action
Faking the sender address to make an email look like it came from a trusted source
Making you feel you must act immediately so you do not stop to think

2.exampleBody: Spot the red flags in this phishing email:
2.exampleCode:
FROM: security@paypa1.com          ← '1' not 'l' — fake domain
SUBJECT: URGENT: Account suspended!

'Dear Valued Customer,             ← No name — mass email
Your PayPal acount has been         ← Spelling error
suspended. Click HERE to restore    ← Suspicious link
your access IMMEDIATELY or your     ← Urgency tactic
funds will be lost FOREVER.'

Real companies never:
— Use urgency to panic you
— Ask for passwords by email
— Have spelling mistakes
2.defaultNote: Show students real examples of phishing emails on the board. The HMRC and 'your parcel' scams are ones they will recognise.

3.starterQuestion:
Your friend says: 'I downloaded a free game from a random website and now my computer is really slow, showing weird adverts, and my files have been renamed with .locked at the end.'

What do you think has happened? What should they do?

keyTerms.def: Malicious software designed to damage, disrupt, or gain unauthorised access to a system
Malware that attaches itself to files and spreads when those files are shared
Malware that encrypts your files and demands payment to restore them
Malware that secretly monitors your activity and sends data to attackers
Malware disguised as legitimate software to trick you into installing it

3.exampleBody: In May 2017, the WannaCry ransomware attacked over 200,000 computers in 150 countries in a single day.
3.exampleCode:
What happened:
— Infected computers had all files encrypted
— A message demanded £230 in Bitcoin
— The NHS in the UK was badly hit
— 80 NHS trusts were affected
— Operations were cancelled
— Ambulances were diverted
— Estimated cost: £92 million to the NHS

How it spread: Unpatched Windows computers
Lesson: ALWAYS install security updates
3.defaultNote: The WannaCry NHS example resonates strongly with students. Ask: 'If a hospital's computers are locked, what happens to patients?'

4.starterQuestion:
You are at McDonald's using the free WiFi. You check your bank balance on your phone.

Why might this be dangerous? What could an attacker do?

keyTerms.def: An unsecured wireless network available in public places — anyone can connect
When an attacker secretly intercepts communication between two parties
A secure version of HTTP that encrypts data sent between your browser and a website
Virtual Private Network — encrypts your internet connection to keep it private
A security system that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic

4.exampleTitle: Public WiFi Attack — How it works
4.exampleBody: Here is how a man-in-the-middle attack works on public WiFi:
4.exampleCode:
Normal connection:
You → [WiFi Router] → [Internet] → Bank website

Attack:
You → [FAKE Router (attacker)] → [Real Router] → Bank

The attacker can see:
✗ Websites you visit
✗ Usernames you type
✗ Passwords you enter
✗ Messages you send

Protection:
✓ Only use HTTPS sites (padlock icon)
✓ Use a VPN on public WiFi
✓ Avoid banking on public networks
4.defaultNote: Ask students to check the sites they use — do they start with https:// or http://? This makes it real and immediate.

5.starterQuestion:
In 2018, Facebook was fined £500,000 for the Cambridge Analytica scandal where data from 87 million users was harvested without consent.

What do you think companies do with your personal data? Why is it valuable?

keyTerms.def: Any information that can identify you — name, address, date of birth, photos, location
When someone uses your personal information to pretend to be you — often for financial gain
When personal data is accessed, stolen, or exposed without authorisation
General Data Protection Regulation — UK/EU law controlling how organisations collect and use personal data
A hidden part of the internet where stolen data is often bought and sold illegally

5.exampleTitle: What does your data sell for?
5.exampleBody: Stolen personal data is bought and sold on the dark web. Here are approximate prices:
5.exampleCode:
Credit card details:       £5 – £20 per card
Online banking login:      £20 – £200
Full identity package:     £150 – £800
(name, DOB, NI, bank, email)
PayPal account access:     £30 – £100
Social media account:      £1 – £10
Email + password combo:    £0.50 – £2

In 2023, 5.5 billion records were stolen
globally — more than one per person on Earth.

Lesson: Your data has real value. Protect it.
5.defaultNote: The dark web prices genuinely shock students and make the abstract concrete. Emphasise: this is why data protection matters.

tasks.title: W1: What Makes a Strong Password?
tasks.question:
LESSON 1 — PASSWORDS & AUTHENTICATION

Your password is the first line of defence against attackers. A weak password can be cracked in seconds.

A strong password should be:
— Long (12+ characters)
— Random (not a word or phrase about you)
— Unique (different for every account)
— Complex (mix of letters, numbers, symbols)

Read each password and select ALL that you would consider STRONG:
options: fluffy123
Tr0ub4dor&3!
correct-horse-battery-staple-42
password
Xk#9mQ2$vL8@
correctAnswers: Tr0ub4dor&3!
correct-horse-battery-staple-42
Xk#9mQ2$vL8@
tasks.markScheme: Award 1 mark per correct answer selected (max 3). Deduct 1 per incorrect selection. Min 0. Strong passwords: Tr0ub4dor&3! (complex+length), correct-horse-battery-staple-42 (very long passphrase), Xk#9mQ2$vL8@ (complex random). Weak: fluffy123 (too simple, short), password (most common password in the world).

tasks.title: W1: Authentication Methods
tasks.question:
LESSON 1 — PASSWORDS & AUTHENTICATION

Passwords alone are not always enough. Many services now use TWO-FACTOR AUTHENTICATION (2FA) — a second check on top of your password.

Examples of 2FA:
🔑 Something you KNOW — a PIN or password
📱 Something you HAVE — a code sent to your phone
👁 Something you ARE — fingerprint or face recognition

Answer ALL of these questions:

1. What is two-factor authentication? Explain it in your own words.

2. Why is 2FA more secure than a password alone? Give a specific reason.

3. A hacker steals your password for your email account. You have 2FA enabled on your phone. Can they access your email? Explain your answer.

4. Some people say '2FA is annoying and slows me down.' Do you think this is a good reason not to use it? Give your view.

5. Name ONE account you personally use where 2FA would be especially important to enable, and explain why.
tasks.markScheme: 1: Clear explanation that 2FA requires two separate proofs of identity — 1 mark. 2: Specific reason e.g. even if password is stolen, attacker still needs the second factor — 1 mark. 3: No — they would need the phone to receive the code — 1 mark. 4: Any reasoned opinion weighing convenience vs security — 1 mark. 5: Any account with personal/financial/sensitive data named with a clear reason — 1 mark.

tasks.title: W1: Password Audit
tasks.question:
LESSON 1 — PRACTICAL TASK

Time to check your own password habits. You do NOT need to share your actual passwords — just answer honestly about your habits.

1. How many different accounts do you have (email, games, social media, school)? Write an approximate number.

2. Do you use the same password for more than one account? Why is this a risk? (Hint: think about what happens if one account is hacked)

3. Create a strong password for a fictional account using the rules from today's lesson. Write it below and explain why it is strong (length, complexity, randomness).
   — Must be 12+ characters
   — Must contain uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and a symbol
   — Must NOT be based on personal information

4. What is a PASSWORD MANAGER and how does it help people use strong, unique passwords for every account?
tasks.markScheme: 1: Any plausible number given honestly — 1 mark. 2: Identifies that if one account is breached, attacker tries same password everywhere (credential stuffing) — 1 mark. 3: A password that genuinely meets all three criteria shown — 1 mark. Explain: must mention at least two of length/complexity/randomness. 4: Software that stores and generates passwords so users only need to remember one master password — 1 mark.

tasks.title: W2: Spot the Phishing Attack
tasks.question:
LESSON 2 — PHISHING & SOCIAL ENGINEERING

Phishing is when criminals send fake messages pretending to be trusted organisations to steal your information.

Read this email carefully:

---
FROM: support@amaz0n-security.com
SUBJECT: ⚠️ URGENT: Your account will be deleted in 24 hours!

Dear Customer,

We have detected suspicious activity on you're account. You must verify your details immediatley by clicking the link below or your account and all purchaces will be permanantly deleted.

[CLICK HERE TO VERIFY YOUR ACCOUNT NOW]

Amazon Security Team
---

Select ALL the red flags that indicate this is a phishing email:
options: The email address uses '0' instead of 'o' in amazon
The email creates a sense of urgency
The email is from Amazon
There are spelling and grammar mistakes
It asks you to click a link to verify details
correctAnswers: The email address uses '0' instead of 'o' in amazon
The email creates a sense of urgency
There are spelling and grammar mistakes
It asks you to click a link to verify details
tasks.markScheme: Award 1 mark per correct red flag identified (max 4 — but question says 3 marks so award 1 per correct up to 3, no deductions for this one). Correct: fake domain, urgency, spelling errors, asking to click link. Incorrect: 'The email is from Amazon' — it is NOT from Amazon.

tasks.title: W2: Social Engineering Tactics
tasks.question:
LESSON 2 — PHISHING & SOCIAL ENGINEERING

Social engineering means manipulating people psychologically rather than hacking computers directly. It exploits human emotions — fear, urgency, curiosity, greed, and trust.

Answer ALL of these:

1. A text message says: 'Your parcel could not be delivered. Pay £1.99 redelivery fee here: bit.ly/parcel-uk.' Millions of people clicked this in 2022. Why do you think so many people fell for it?

2. A caller says they are from your bank's fraud department and says there has been suspicious activity on your account. They ask you to 'confirm' your card number for security. What should you do and why?

3. What is SPEAR PHISHING? How is it more dangerous than regular phishing?

4. A pop-up on a website says 'CONGRATULATIONS! You are the 1,000,000th visitor! Click here to claim your prize!' What type of social engineering tactic is this and what might happen if you click?

5. Describe TWO ways schools and workplaces try to protect people from phishing attacks.
tasks.markScheme: 1: Convincing cover story, expected behaviour (parcel deliveries common), small amount seems low risk, urgency — 1 mark for any two valid reasons. 2: Hang up and call the bank's official number directly — never confirm details to an inbound caller — 1 mark. 3: Targeted attack using personal information to seem more convincing — more dangerous because harder to detect — 1 mark. 4: Greed/excitement tactic — clicking could install malware, steal data, or lead to a fake prize scam — 1 mark. 5: Two valid methods e.g. staff training, spam filters, email warnings, simulated phishing tests, reporting systems — 1 mark.

tasks.title: W3: Malware & Ransomware
tasks.question:
LESSON 3 — MALWARE & VIRUSES

Malware is any software designed to damage or gain unauthorised access to a system. There are many types.

Match each description to the correct type of malware, then answer the questions below:

Types: VIRUS / RANSOMWARE / SPYWARE / TROJAN HORSE / WORM

1. Match each description:
   A) Encrypts your files and demands payment to unlock them
   B) Secretly records your keystrokes and sends them to attackers
   C) Disguised as a legitimate app — installs when you think you're installing something else
   D) Spreads automatically across a network without needing a host file
   E) Attaches to files and spreads when those files are shared

2. The NHS was hit by ransomware in 2017. Why is a hospital a particularly serious target for ransomware compared to, say, a small shop?

3. Name THREE ways you can protect yourself from malware.

4. Someone downloads a 'free' version of an expensive game from an unofficial website. Why is this especially risky?
tasks.markScheme: 1: A=Ransomware, B=Spyware, C=Trojan Horse, D=Worm, E=Virus — 1 mark for all 5 correct, 0 marks if more than 2 wrong. 2: Lives depend on hospital systems — operations cancelled, patient data at risk, life-threatening consequences — 1 mark. 3: Any three from: antivirus software, keeping software updated, not downloading from untrusted sources, not clicking suspicious links, regular backups — 1 mark. 4: Free pirated software commonly contains trojans or spyware hidden in the installer — attackers use greed as the attack vector — 1 mark.

tasks.title: W4: Network Security
tasks.question:
LESSON 4 — NETWORK SECURITY & PUBLIC WIFI

When you connect to a network — especially a public one — your data can be intercepted.

Answer ALL of these:

1. What is a MAN-IN-THE-MIDDLE ATTACK? Draw a simple text diagram showing how it works (you can use arrows and labels like: You → Attacker → Internet).

2. You are in a coffee shop. You see two WiFi networks: 'CoffeeShop_Free' and 'CoffeeShop Free WiFi'. How could you tell which one is genuine? Why might this matter?

3. What does the padlock icon and 'https://' in a browser address bar mean? Why does it help protect you?

4. What is a VPN and when should you use one?

5. Your school network has a firewall that blocks certain websites. Some students think this is unfair. Give ONE argument FOR school firewalls and ONE argument AGAINST.
tasks.markScheme: 1: Clear explanation that attacker intercepts traffic between user and destination + any reasonable text diagram — 1 mark. 2: A fake hotspot with a similar name could be set up by an attacker — should confirm with staff or use mobile data — 1 mark. 3: HTTPS encrypts data between browser and server so interceptors cannot read it — 1 mark. 4: Encrypts all internet traffic, hides your real IP, should use on public WiFi especially — 1 mark. 5: FOR — protects students from harmful content, malware, legal liability. AGAINST — restricts learning, treats students as suspects, blocks legitimate resources — 1 mark for both sides.

tasks.title: W5: Personal Data & Identity Theft
tasks.question:
LESSON 5 — PERSONAL DATA & IDENTITY THEFT

Your personal data is valuable. Criminals collect it to steal your identity, access your accounts, or sell it.

Answer ALL of these:

1. What is IDENTITY THEFT? Give a specific example of how a criminal might use your personal data.

2. Look at a typical social media profile. List FIVE pieces of information that someone could use to build a profile of you or guess your passwords.

3. In 2021, the personal data of 533 million Facebook users was leaked online. Why do data breaches like this matter even if you 'have nothing to hide'?

4. Under UK GDPR, you have the 'Right to Erasure' (also called the Right to be Forgotten). What does this mean and when can you use it?

5. You receive an email saying 'We found your email and password on the dark web. Change your password immediately at this link.' How do you verify if this is genuine or a phishing attack?
tasks.markScheme: 1: Clear definition + specific example e.g. using DOB + address to apply for a credit card in your name — 1 mark. 2: Five valid items e.g. name, school, birthday, hometown, pet name, relationships, phone number, interests — 1 mark (need 4+). 3: Data can be used for phishing, identity theft, targeting, emotional harm — privacy protects everyone — 1 mark. 4: The right to ask an organisation to delete your personal data — can use when data is no longer necessary or consent is withdrawn — 1 mark. 5: Go directly to haveibeenpwned.com, do NOT click the link in the email, check the sender address, change password via the official site directly — 1 mark.

tasks.title: W6: Build Your Presentation
tasks.question:
LESSON 6 — BUILD YOUR PRESENTATION

You have learned about five cyber security topics over the past 5 weeks. Now it is time to build your 10-minute presentation for {subject}.

Your presentation MUST include ALL of the following:
✅ A clear title and introduction (who you are, what you will cover)
✅ At least THREE of the five topics covered (passwords, phishing, malware, networks, personal data)
✅ For each topic: what it is, a real-world example, and how to stay safe
✅ At least ONE statistic or real-world fact per topic
✅ A summary slide with your TOP 5 cyber security tips for your audience
✅ Clear, appropriate design for {subject}
✅ Speaker notes or a script (so you know what to say on each slide)

Step 1: Build your presentation in Canva or Google Slides.
Step 2: Paste your presentation link below.
